title: Statistics - Lesson 3: Claims and Displays Practice
description: Practice matching statistical claims to displays, evidence, and careful conclusions.

questions.question: A claim says, "Most students chose online review." Which information is most important to check first?
options: The number who chose online review and the total number surveyed
The color used for the online review bar
Whether the graph has a decorative title
The order of the answer choices on the survey
questions.explanation: "Most" means more than half, so you need both the part and the whole group.

questions.question: Which display is usually best for supporting a claim about quiz averages changing from Monday to Friday?
questions.explanation: A line graph is designed to show change over time or ordered intervals.

questions.question: A graph can be technically accurate but still make a small difference look dramatic.
questions.explanation: A shortened or uneven scale can exaggerate visual differences even when the plotted values are accurate.

questions.question: In a survey of 50 learners, 30 preferred group review. What percent preferred group review? Enter a percent such as 60%.
A bar graph compares 72% and 75%, but its vertical axis starts at 70%. What is the best warning?
options: The 3-point difference may look larger than it really is
The graph proves there is no difference
questions.explanation: Starting the axis near the data can stretch the bars visually and make a small gap look large.

questions.question: The largest category in a table is always more than half of the total.
questions.explanation: A category can be the largest and still be less than 50% if the responses are spread across several categories.

questions.question: A poster says, "Grade 10 students love the new schedule," based on 9 students from one club. In one sentence, explain a weakness in the claim.
questions.correctAnswer: The sample is small and from only one club, so it may not represent all Grade 10 students.
questions.explanation: A strong response should mention the mismatch between the broad claim and the narrow sample.

questions.question: Write a careful conclusion for this evidence: 18 out of 40 surveyed students preferred printed modules, while 16 preferred online review.
questions.correctAnswer: Printed modules were the most selected option in this sample, but the lead over online review was small.
questions.explanation: The conclusion should use the evidence and avoid overstating the 2-student difference.
